hints: Notice that $R_1$ and $R_2$ in series form one branch in parallel with $R_3$, so both branches have p.d. $1.60 \, \text{V}$.
Use Kirchhoff's first law at the junction: $0.64 \, \text{A}$ from the cell splits into $0.32 \, \text{A}$ through $R_3$, leaving $0.32 \, \text{A}$ through $R_1$ and $R_2$.
Subtract the $0.48 \, \text{V}$ across $R_1$ from the $1.60 \, \text{V}$ branch p.d. to get the p.d. across $R_2$, then apply $R = V/I$.
walkthrough: Identify the branches: the middle branch contains $R_1$ and $R_2$ in series, and the lower branch contains $R_3$. The two branches are in parallel across the $1.60 \, \text{V}$ cell of negligible internal resistance.

Find the current in the $R_1$-$R_2$ branch using Kirchhoff's first law. Total cell current is $0.64 \, \text{A}$ and current in $R_3$ is $0.32 \, \text{A}$, so $I = 0.64 - 0.32 = 0.32 \, \text{A}$ flows through $R_1$ and $R_2$ in series.
Find the p.d. across $R_2$ using Kirchhoff's second law around the middle loop. The branch p.d. equals the e.m.f., $1.60 \, \text{V}$, so $V_{R1} + V_{R2} = 1.60 \, \text{V}$.
Apply $R = V/I$ to $R_2$: $R_2 = 1.12 \, \text{V} / 0.32 \, \text{A} = 3.5 \, \Omega$, with unit check $\text{V A}^{-1} = \Omega$. This is option C.

options.A: Gives $0.48/0.32 = 1.5 \, \Omega$, which is the resistance of $R_1$, not $R_2$.
options.B: Uses only part of the $1.60 \, \text{V}$ across the $R_1$-$R_2$ branch, giving too small a p.d. for $R_2$.
options.C: The p.d. across $R_2$ is $1.60 - 0.48 = 1.12 \, \text{V}$ with current $0.32 \, \text{A}$, so $R_2 = 1.12/0.32 = 3.5 \, \Omega$.
options.D: Gives $1.60/0.32 = 5.0 \, \Omega$, which is the combined resistance of $R_1 + R_2$, not $R_2$ alone.
